name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,732

clue.text: Relative laughter and wit mostly confused

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped
confused letters are muddled up and must be put back into a new order

blocks.note: the word wit without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone baffled by a family member's giggling and half-formed jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative' could be an adjective, but it is the noun definition. All thirteen letters of the fodder, including the conjunction, are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A son's wife is a family member by marriage, so she counts as one of your kin.

clue.text: Obedient duke you almost argue with close to Malibu lake

indicators.note: almost means falling just short, so the final letter goes
the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is kept

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for duke
U sounds like 'you', as in text-speak
to tiff is to quarrel; the word loses its last letter
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A compliant aristocrat squabbling beside a lake in California.
explanation.walkthrough: TIFF, a minor quarrel, is a verb as well as a noun, so it fits 'argue'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who does what duty requires and follows orders is compliant, a close synonym.

clue.text: Parasite infecting American military groups

indicators.note: something that infects gets inside a host, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: US is the abbreviation for American
a nit is a louse egg, a parasite

explanation.surface: A bug spreading through the US armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: The insect goes inside the two-letter abbreviation for the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Army detachments such as battalions and companies are called formations or units in military usage.

clue.text: Unusual bush elm makes appear small?

indicators.note: unusual means out of the normal order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd shrub dwarfing a tree beside it in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is loose: humbling makes a person feel small rather than look physically small.
explanation.definitionFit: To humble someone is to lower their pride or status, diminishing them in others' eyes.

clue.text: Poem primarily evoking country life of good utopian existence?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is taken

blocks.clueFragment: evoking country life of good utopian existence
blocks.note: the initial letters of these seven words

explanation.surface: A description of a pastoral verse idealising rural life.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay also describes the answer: such poems really do evoke an idealised country life.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a short pastoral verse form, often a dialogue between shepherds, as written by Virgil.

clue.text: Underwriter certain to be taken on by hip head of recruitment

indicators.note: to be taken on is to be absorbed into something, so one piece goes inside another
the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: in means fashionable, as hip does

explanation.surface: An underwriter sure of being hired by a trendy head of recruiting.
explanation.walkthrough: The four-letter word goes between the two letters of the word for trendy, then the initial is added.
explanation.definitionFit: An underwriter accepts liability for risks in return for premiums, which is what such a company does.

clue.text: Odious bunch around a house eating seconds

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece is placed within another
something eating takes food inside it, so one piece is swallowed by another

blocks.note: a lot is a group or bunch
S is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A horrible gang hanging about a house, wolfing down second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like extra helpings of food but is just the unit abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something hateful, disgusting or repellent, so they are straight synonyms.

clue.text: Footballer dropping head could make folk tearful!

indicators.note: dropping the head of a word removes its first letter

blocks.note: a sweeper is a defender who plays behind the back line

explanation.surface: A footballer hanging his head in defeat brings the fans to tears.
explanation.walkthrough: A sweeper is a football position, a free defender covering behind the others. The definition reads as 'tearful folk'.
explanation.definitionFit: People who cry are mourners or criers, so a plural noun for those who shed tears fits.

clue.text: Belt everyone gets in Mississippi shopping centres

indicators.note: getting in means entering something, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a belt is a long narrow band or strip, as in a belt of land
MS is the postal code for Mississippi

explanation.surface: Everyone in Mississippi wearing a belt to the shopping centres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belt' could be a verb meaning hit or a garment, but here it is a band of territory.
explanation.definitionFit: These are American roadside retail developments, a row of shops sharing a car park.

clue.text: A man with first sign of mould-induced cough

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A man in a damp house develops a cough caused by mould.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mould-induced' reads as one adjective, but it splits into the source of a letter and a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: This interjection represents the small throat-clearing noise made to attract attention.

clue.text: American kills posh people without right ultimately

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is taken away
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is used

explanation.surface: An American murdering members of the upper class, regardless of what is right.
explanation.walkthrough: Toff is British slang for a posh person. The final letter of 'right' is removed from the front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: In US slang 'to off' someone is to murder them, so the third-person verb form matches.

clue.text: Out-of-control rabbit mauled a horologer

indicators.note: something mauled is torn about and mangled, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wild rabbit has savaged a clockmaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' is British slang for chatter (to rabbit on is to talk endlessly), so it is not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: This medical term means excessive, uncontrollable talkativeness, endless chatter running away with itself.

clue.text: Connoisseurs swallowing large lies

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Experts gullibly accepting big fibs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallowing' suggests believing the lies, but it is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluff is a pretence or deception meant to mislead, so the plural noun fits untruths.

clue.text: Soldiers in new airlift will get access to blaze in Oz?

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another
new suggests a fresh arrangement, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Troops flown in by air reach a bushfire in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oz' is Australia, where the term comes from; the question mark marks a definition by description.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australia, a track cleared through bush gives firefighting vehicles a route to reach wildfires.

clue.text: Nurse goes off to collect old implants

indicators.note: to collect is to gather in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A nurse leaves to pick up an elderly patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes off' looks like departing, but it means spoiling.
explanation.definitionFit: To fix something firmly in place, like planting it so it takes hold, is to establish it deeply.

clue.text: Fruit of month not entirely firm, having touch of tenderness

indicators.note: not entirely means missing a part, so the last letter is cut
a touch is the smallest amount, just the first letter

blocks.note: the month April loses its last letter
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: Seasonal fruit, slightly hard but with a little give when pressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like part of a description of ripeness, but it is a company.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an orange stone fruit related to the plum and peach.

clue.text: A conservative assertion gets much praise

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A right-wing statement wins plenty of applause.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C stands for a Conservative, Britain's main right-of-centre party.
explanation.definitionFit: Acclaim is enthusiastic public approval, applause or acclamation, so it means lavish commendation.

clue.text: Nightspot with live band at last hit with staff?

indicators.note: at last means at the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: to be is to live or exist

explanation.surface: A nightclub with live music is a hit with its employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit with staff' reads like popular with employees, but a staff here is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A club is a heavy stick, so being beaten with a cudgel or similar rod means this.

clue.text: Type of engine in Ford model Triumph briefly advanced

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the Model T was Ford's famous early car
came, meaning advanced, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Comparing the engines in Ford and Triumph cars.
explanation.walkthrough: Triumph is a British car maker, so it reads as a brand, but it means a victory.
explanation.definitionFit: This engine design has two camshafts operating the valves, a common performance layout.

clue.text: Information gathered by a vacuous city bureau

indicators.note: what is gathered is held inside, so one piece sits within others
vacuous means empty, so the inside letters go and only the outer pair remain

explanation.surface: Intelligence collected by an empty-headed municipal office.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is British slang for information, as in getting the gen on something.
explanation.definitionFit: An office or organisation providing a particular service, such as a travel agency, is a bureau.

clue.text: Craftsperson is prejudiced, having dismissed Penny

indicators.note: dismissing sends something away, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for penny

explanation.surface: A biased worker who has sacked a woman called Penny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny' looks like a name, but it is the coin abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A skilled manual worker who makes things by hand is a craftsman or artisan.

clue.text: Republican gets roasted about being corrupt

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A Republican politician is grilled over allegations of corruption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roasted' suggests harsh criticism, but it is a kitchen word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishonest or fraudulent in slang terms, a bent official is described this way.

clue.text: Doctor cries out to green holidaymaker

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or alter, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A doctor calls out to an inexperienced tourist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a physician and 'green' like naive; one is the anagram signal and the other means environmentally minded.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone travelling in an environmentally responsible way, to natural areas, is a sustainable traveller.

clue.text: British express disapproval about gaffe

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the word faces the other way

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
to boo is to jeer in disapproval

explanation.surface: Britons jeering at a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: The jeer is turned back to front after the initial letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Boob is informal British slang for a silly mistake or blunder.

clue.text: Pop hit from America covering Queen

indicators.note: covering means wrapping round, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: bust is American slang for a punch or hit
R is for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: An American chart hit doing a cover of a Queen song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop hit' and 'Queen' summon music, but 'Pop' is a verb definition and Queen is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: When a balloon pops, it explodes or bursts suddenly with a bang.

clue.text: Indian Melody Maker paper article

blocks.note: a rag is slang for a newspaper

explanation.surface: An Indian edition of the old British music weekly Melody Maker.
explanation.walkthrough: Melody Maker was a British music paper; the title splits so the first word joins the definition and the second is padding before the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In Indian classical music this is a melodic framework on which a performer improvises.

clue.text: Support city welcoming Republican movement a swimmer might start?

indicators.note: to welcome is to let in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: Stoke-on-Trent is a city in Staffordshire
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: Backing a city that is welcoming a political campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement' reads as a political movement, but it is a swimming action; Stoke is an English city.
explanation.definitionFit: This swimming style, done on the back, is the stroke a swimmer could begin with.

clue.text: Awfully old idea Met man's run by men?

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A dated notion held by a Metropolitan Police officer that institutions should be run by men.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met is London's Metropolitan Police. The apostrophe-s stands for 'is' and links the anagram to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An organisation controlled chiefly by men, with women excluded from power, is described this way.
